Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) was rejected for every tested request, including north/south/east regions, refunds, shipments, claims, small and large amounts, and requests mentioning regional offices. Do not select C based solely on region or wording.
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for REQ-2409: small shipment, north region, requester said the client had asked twice already. This suggests repeated/urgent follow-up may justify B, but evidence is limited to one case.
- Requester department, sender surname, and phrases such as “second attempt,” “no rush,” or “confirm receipt” have not yet established routing rules.
- No evidence yet for A (standard queue) or D (external partner).
- Treat request attributes (type, size, region, urgency/history) as relevant, but do not infer that the originating channel or regional-office mention determines the route.

Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) has been rejected in all tested cases, including region-based requests and requests explicitly saying they came through a regional office. Do not select C solely because of region, wording, or channel.
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for REQ-2409 (small north shipment, repeated request) and REQ-2410 (small east invoice, second attempt after bounced form). However, B was rejected for a small south shipment with the same “second attempt” wording and for an urgent small south claim. Repeated/urgent wording may help but is not sufficient.
- Option A (standard queue) succeeded for small south refunds from Field Sales and Regional Ops when marked “no rush, but please confirm receipt.” The same request details and wording were rejected for Client Services, so requester identity/department appears relevant.
- A was rejected for requests mentioning regional-office intake, scanned paperwork, and a large east invoice; do not assume standard handling for these.
- A was also rejected for a small north claim with regional-office wording.
- Requester department, sender surname, request type/size/region, urgency/history, intake wording, and document format may all affect routing. No single factor is decisive yet.
- No positive evidence for D (external partner).
- Treat each new combination as uncertain; avoid generalizing from one accepted ticket.

Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case, including region-based and explicitly regional-office intake requests. Do not select C based on region, wording, or channel.
- Option D (external partner) has no positive evidence. It was rejected for a large north shipment from Partner Accounts; department alone does not justify D.
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for REQ-2409 (small north shipment, repeated request), REQ-2410 (small east invoice, bounced form), and REQ-2421 (large north claim, Regional Ops, “same as last month”). It was rejected for multiple recent large refunds, shipments, and small claims, including repeated/urgent requests. B is not generally indicated by urgency, repetition, size, or region.
- Option A (standard queue) succeeded for small south refunds from Field Sales and Regional Ops marked “no rush, but please confirm receipt.” It was rejected for a Partner Accounts small south claim with end-of-day wording and for several regional-office, scanned-paperwork, large-invoice, and north-claim cases.
- Recent failures suggest requester department/identity may be highly influential: Regional Ops produced one B success but also one B failure; Partner Accounts produced failures with A, B, and D. Do not infer routing from department alone.
- Large requests have not established a general route: large north claim succeeded with B, while large north refund/shipment and large south refunds failed with B/D.
- Requester department, surname, request type/size/region, urgency/history, intake wording, and document format may interact. No single factor is decisive.
- Treat every new combination as uncertain; avoid generalizing from one accepted ticket.

Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) still has no positive evidence and was rejected in every tested case. Do not select C based on region or “came through the regional office” wording.
- Option D (external partner) has no positive evidence; department alone does not justify it.
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for REQ-2409, REQ-2410, and REQ-2421, but failed for large/small claims, refunds, shipments, and invoices across multiple departments, regions, and urgency/repetition patterns. Do not infer B from urgency, repetition, size, region, or request type.
- Option A (standard queue) succeeded for small south refunds with “no rush,” and notably for REQ-2430: a large north shipment from Field Sales whose requester said it came through the regional office. A failed for many other combinations, including urgent small east claim, regional-office small north refund, repeated small east refund, Partner Accounts small north claim, and several large/invoice/claim cases.
- Recent examples strengthen the evidence that interactions matter: Field Sales + regional-office wording + large north shipment favored A, while similar regional-office wording with small north refunds failed under A. Regional-office wording does not imply C.
- Partner Accounts has produced failures with A, B, and D; Client Services has produced B failures across large/small claims, refunds, and invoices. Department remains insufficient alone.
- Large requests have no stable route: A succeeded once for a large shipment, while B failed for large claim/invoice cases and prior large requests.
- Document format, intake wording, requester identity/department, request type, size, region, urgency, and history likely interact. Treat each new combination as uncertain; avoid generalizing from isolated successes or failures.

Routing lessons:

- Option D (external partner) has no positive evidence; department alone does not justify it. It also failed for a large east refund from Partner Accounts (REQ-2443).
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for REQ-2409, REQ-2410, and REQ-2421, but failed for large/small claims, refunds, shipments, and invoices across multiple departments, regions, and urgency/repetition patterns. Do not infer B from urgency, repetition, size, region, or request type.
- Option A (standard queue) has now failed across many combinations. New failures include Client Services large east claim; Finance Desk small/large claims, large north shipment, large east invoice, and small north claim; Partner Accounts large east claim and small south invoice; and Field Sales small north invoice. Do not generalize from its isolated successes (small south refund with “no rush,” or REQ-2430’s large north shipment).
- “No rush,” end-of-day urgency, confirmation requests, missing-information wording, repeated submissions, and client follow-up have not reliably identified a route. These notes may interact with department, request type, size, region, and format, but current evidence is insufficient.
- Regional-office wording does not imply C; Field Sales + that wording + a large north shipment favored A once, while similar small north refunds did not.
- Partner Accounts has produced failures with A, B, and D; Client Services has produced B and A failures. Finance Desk and Field Sales now also show A failures. Department remains insufficient alone.
- Treat every new combination as uncertain; avoid selecting any option from a single feature or isolated success.

- Option A (standard queue) now has extensive failures across departments, regions, sizes, request types, and wording. New failures include Field Sales large south refund; Regional Ops small south refunds and small east shipment; Client Services small east invoice and small south shipment; Partner Accounts large east invoice; and Field Sales small east refund. Its isolated successes must not be generalized.
- “No rush,” end-of-day urgency, confirmation requests, missing-information wording, repeated submissions/client follow-up, regional-office wording, and scanned-versus-typed paperwork have not reliably identified a route.
- Regional Ops now also shows A failures; Partner Accounts has failures with A, B, and D; Client Services has B and A failures; Finance Desk and Field Sales have A failures. Department remains insufficient alone.
